title: Oscillations (Simple Harmonic Motion)
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: SHM Differential Equation, Phasor Circle Diagram, Kinetic & Potential Energy in SHM, Spring Combinations, Simple/Compound/Torsional Pendulums, U-Tube & Earth-Tunnel SHM, Damped & Forced Resonance
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: Periodic vs. Oscillatory vs. Simple Harmonic Motion

Look around you: the Earth orbits the Sun every $365.25$ days, your heart beats roughly once every second, a guitar string vibrates back and forth, and a pendulum swings from side to side. All of these repeat themselves in time, yet they are not all the same type of motion!

The 3-Level Hierarchy of Repeating Motion:
  • 1. Periodic Motion: Any motion that repeats itself at regular intervals of time $T$ (e.g., Earth orbiting the Sun, hands of a clock). It does NOT have to move back and forth!
  • 2. Oscillatory (Vibratory) Motion: A periodic motion in which a body moves back and forth (to and fro) repeatedly about a fixed stable equilibrium point (Mean Position), where $F_{\text{net}} = 0$ and potential energy $U(x)$ is a local minimum ($F = -k x^n$ where $n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$).
  • 3. Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM): The simplest and most fundamental special case of oscillatory motion in which the restoring force (and acceleration) is directly proportional to the first power ($n = 1$) of displacement from the mean position and always directed toward the mean position: $$\boxed{F = -k x \iff a = -\omega^2 x}$$
Every SHM is oscillatory, and every oscillatory motion is periodic—but not every periodic motion is SHM!

topics.title: Kinematics of SHM: Differential Equation, Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration & The Phasor Circle Method
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 The Master Equations of Linear SHM
$$\textbf{Standard Differential Equation of SHM:} \qquad \boxed{\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2 x = 0} \qquad \left(\text{where } \omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \frac{2\pi}{T} = 2\pi f\right)$$
QuantityAs a Function of Time ($t$)As a Function of Position ($x$)At Mean ($x = 0$)At Extreme ($x = \pm A$)
Displacement ($x$)$x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$x$$0$$\pm A$ (Max)
Velocity ($v = \frac{dx}{dt}$)$v(t) = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi)$
$= A\omega\sin\left(\omega t + \phi + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$		$$\boxed{v(x) = \pm\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}}$$$\pm A\omega$ (Max)$0$ (Min)
Acceleration ($a = \frac{dv}{dt}$)$a(t) = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t + \phi)$
$= A\omega^2\sin(\omega t + \phi + \pi)$		$$\boxed{a(x) = -\omega^2 x}$$$0$ (Min)$\mp A\omega^2$ (Max)

Phase Lead Relations: Velocity $v(t)$ leads displacement $x(t)$ by phase angle $\mathbf{\frac{\pi}{2}}$ ($90^\circ$), and acceleration $a(t)$ leads velocity by $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and is completely out of phase with displacement by $\mathbf{\pi}$ ($180^\circ$).

1.2 Uniform Circular Motion Projection (The Phasor Circle Shortcut)
How to Solve Any “Time Taken from $x_1$ to $x_2$” Question in 10 Seconds:
SHM is the exact shadow (projection) on a diameter of a particle moving in a circle of radius $A$ at constant angular speed $\omega$! Since $\omega$ is constant on the reference circle, the time taken to move between two positions $x_1$ and $x_2$ is simply the angular travel $\Delta\theta$ divided by $\omega$: $$\boxed{\Delta t = \frac{\Delta\theta}{\omega} = \left(\frac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi}\right)T}$$
  • From Mean ($x = 0$) to Half-Amplitude ($x = A/2$): $\sin\theta = \frac{1}{2} \implies \Delta\theta = \frac{\pi}{6}$ ($30^\circ$) $\implies \boxed{t_1 = \frac{\pi/6}{2\pi}T = \frac{T}{12}}$.
  • From Half-Amplitude ($x = A/2$) to Extreme ($x = A$): $\Delta\theta = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\pi}{3}$ ($60^\circ$) $\implies \boxed{t_2 = \frac{T}{6} = 2t_1}$! (Takes twice as long because the particle slows down near the extreme!)
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation of v(x) = ±ω√(A² − x²) & The v-x Ellipse Equation

Using $a = v\frac{dv}{dx} = -\omega^2 x$, separate variables and integrate from the extreme position $(x = A, v = 0)$ to $(x, v)$:

$$\int_0^v v\,dv = -\omega^2 \int_A^x x\,dx \implies \frac{v^2}{2} = \frac{\omega^2(A^2 - x^2)}{2} \implies \boxed{v = \pm\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}}$$

Rearranging $v^2 = \omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$ gives the equation of the Velocity-Displacement ($v$-$x$) Phase-Space Curve:

$$\boxed{\frac{x^2}{A^2} + \frac{v^2}{(A\omega)^2} = 1} \qquad (\text{An ELLIPSE with semi-axes } A \text{ and } A\omega\text{!})$$

Defining shifted coordinate $X = x - 4$ gives $F = -3(x - 4) = -3X$, which is pure SHM with $\omega = \sqrt{3/m}$ about the new mean position $x_{\text{mean}} = 4$!

topics.title: Kinetic, Potential & Total Energy in SHM, Energy Frequency (2f) & Superposition of SHMs
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 Kinetic Energy ($K$), Potential Energy ($U$) & Total Energy ($E$) in SHM

Let potential energy at the mean position ($x = 0$) be $U_0$ (usually taken as $U_0 = 0$). Since $k = m\omega^2$:

$$\begin{aligned} \text{1. Potential Energy:} & \quad \boxed{U(x) = U_0 + \frac{1}{2}k x^2 = U_0 + \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2 \sin^2(\omega t + \phi)} \\[6pt] \text{2. Kinetic Energy:} & \quad \boxed{K(x) = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2) = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2 \cos^2(\omega t + \phi)} \\[6pt] \text{3. Total Mechanical Energy:} & \quad \boxed{E = K + U = U_0 + \frac{1}{2}k A^2 = U_0 + \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 A^2 = U_0 + 2\pi^2 m f^2 A^2} \end{aligned}$$
  • Where Does $K = U$ (assuming $U_0 = 0$)? Set $\frac{1}{2}k(A^2 - x^2) = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 \implies 2x^2 = A^2 \implies \boxed{x = \pm\frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}}$ (and at $t = \frac{T}{8}$ from mean position!).
  • Frequency of $K$ and $U$ is $2f$ (Double the SHM Frequency!):
    Using $\cos^2(\omega t) = \frac{1 + \cos(2\omega t)}{2}$, both Kinetic Energy $K(t)$ and Potential Energy $U(t)$ oscillate with angular frequency $\mathbf{2\omega}$ (frequency $\mathbf{2f}$, time period $\mathbf{T/2}$), whereas Total Energy $E$ has frequency $0$ (constant)!
  • Time-Average vs. Space-Average Over One Complete Cycle (assuming $U_0 = 0$):
    $$\text{Time Average (with respect to } t\text{):} \quad \boxed{\langle K \rangle_t = \langle U \rangle_t = \frac{1}{4}kA^2 = \frac{E}{2}}$$
    $$\text{Space Average (with respect to } x\text{):} \quad \boxed{\langle U \rangle_x = \frac{1}{A}\int_0^A \frac{1}{2}kx^2\,dx = \frac{1}{6}kA^2 = \frac{E}{3}, \qquad \langle K \rangle_x = \frac{1}{3}kA^2 = \frac{2E}{3}}$$
2.2 Superposition of Two Collinear SHMs of Same Frequency

If a particle is simultaneously subjected to $x_1 = A_1\sin(\omega t)$ and $x_2 = A_2\sin(\omega t + \delta)$, the resultant motion $x = x_1 + x_2 = A_{\text{res}}\sin(\omega t + \alpha)$ is also SHM of the same frequency $\omega$, found by treating $A_1$ and $A_2$ as vectors separated by angle $\delta$:

$$\boxed{A_{\text{res}} = \sqrt{A_1^2 + A_2^2 + 2 A_1 A_2 \cos\delta}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \boxed{\tan\alpha = \frac{A_2\sin\delta}{A_1 + A_2\cos\delta}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
How to Find Time Period of Any Conservative System Using the Energy Method (dE/dt = 0)

Whenever a system involves springs, pulleys, and rolling cylinders where force/torque equations look messy, use the Energy Conservation Derivative Trick:

Step 1: Write the total mechanical energy $E = K + U$ in terms of speed $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$ and displacement $x$:
$$E = \frac{1}{2}m_{\text{eff}} v^2 + \frac{1}{2}k_{\text{eff}} x^2 = \text{Constant}$$

Step 2: Differentiate with respect to time $t$ ($\frac{dE}{dt} = 0$) and cancel $v = \frac{dx}{dt}$:

$$m_{\text{eff}} v\frac{dv}{dt} + k_{\text{eff}} x\frac{dx}{dt} = 0 \implies \frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \left(\frac{k_{\text{eff}}}{m_{\text{eff}}}\right)x = 0 \implies \boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m_{\text{eff}}}{k_{\text{eff}}}}}$$

topics.title: Spring-Block Systems: Series/Parallel Springs, Cutting a Spring, Two-Body Reduced Mass & Pulley-Spring SHM
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 Spring Combinations & Cutting a Spring ($k \cdot L = \text{Constant}$)
Why Constant Forces (Like Gravity $mg$ or Electric Field $qE$) NEVER Change the Time Period of a Spring-Block System:
Hanging a block vertically on a spring stretches the equilibrium position downward by $x_0 = mg/k$, but the restoring force for an additional displacement $x$ from this new equilibrium is STILL $F_{\text{net}} = mg - k(x_0 + x) = -kx$! Thus $\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}}$ is completely independent of $g$, incline angle $\theta$, or elevator acceleration!
Spring ConfigurationEquivalent Spring Constant ($k_{\text{eq}}$)Resulting Time Period ($T$)
1. Parallel Combination
(Both springs experience same extension $x$)		$$\boxed{k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2}$$$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_1 + k_2}}$$
2. Series Combination
(Both springs carry same tension $F$)		$$\boxed{\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2} \implies k_{\text{eq}} = \frac{k_1 k_2}{k_1 + k_2}}$$$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m(k_1 + k_2)}{k_1 k_2}} = \sqrt{T_1^2 + T_2^2}$$
3. Cutting a Spring of Stiffness $k$ and Length $L$Since $k = \frac{YA}{L} \implies \boxed{k L = \text{Constant}}$!
If cut into lengths $L_1$ and $L_2$:		$$k_1 = k\left(\frac{L}{L_1}\right), \quad k_2 = k\left(\frac{L}{L_2}\right)$$
(A shorter piece of spring is ALWAYS stiffer!)
4. Two Masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ Connected by Spring $k$ on Smooth FloorOscillates about COM with Reduced Mass $\mu$:
$$\boxed{\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}}$$		$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m_1 m_2}{(m_1 + m_2)k}}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Constraint Shortcut for Pulley-Spring Systems: k_eff = k (x_spring / x_block)²

Suppose a block of mass $m$ is attached to a movable pulley while a spring of constant $k$ is attached to the string or pulley axle. How do you find $k_{\text{eff}}$ instantly?

Step 1: Displace the mass $m$ by $x_m$, and use string constraint ($\sum T \cdot x = 0$) to find the extension $x_s$ of the spring.

Step 2: By virtual work / energy conservation ($\frac{1}{2}k_{\text{eff}} x_m^2 = \frac{1}{2}k x_s^2$):

$$\boxed{k_{\text{eff}} = k \left(\frac{x_s}{x_m}\right)^2}$$

Example 1: If pulling the block by $x$ stretches the spring by $2x$ ($x_s = 2x_m$), then $k_{\text{eff}} = 4k$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{4k}}$.
Example 2: If pulling the block by $x$ stretches the spring by $x/2$ ($x_s = x_m / 2$), then $k_{\text{eff}} = \frac{k}{4}$ and $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{4m}{k}}$!

topics.jeeTraps: • Trap (Block Sandwiched Between Two Springs Connected to Two Walls): Looking at the left diagram above, students think the two springs $k_1$ and $k_2$ on opposite sides of block $m$ are in series. NO! When the block moves right by $x$, spring $k_1$ stretches by $x$ (pulling left with $k_1 x$) and spring $k_2$ compresses by $x$ (pushing left with $k_2 x$). Since their restoring forces ADD ($F = -(k_1 + k_2)x$), they are in PARALLEL ($k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$)!

topics.title: Simple, Compound & Torsional Pendulums, U-Tube & Earth-Tunnel SHM, Damped & Forced Oscillations
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Simple Pendulum & Effective Gravity ($g_{\text{eff}}$) in All Frames
$$\text{Small-Angle Simple Pendulum } (\theta \le 10^\circ): \qquad \boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{\text{eff}}}}}$$

What Is $g_{\text{eff}}$ in Different Situations? (General rule: $g_{\text{eff}} = \frac{\text{Tension } T_0 \text{ at equilibrium}}{m}$)

  • 1. Elevator accelerating upward at $a_0$: $g_{\text{eff}} = g + a_0$; accelerating downward at $a_0$: $g_{\text{eff}} = g - a_0$; in free fall / orbiting satellite: $g_{\text{eff}} = 0 \implies \mathbf{T = \infty}$ (does not oscillate!).
  • 2. Car accelerating horizontally at $a_0$: $\boxed{g_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{g^2 + a_0^2}}$ (mean position tilts backward by $\tan\theta = a_0/g$).
  • 3. Cart sliding frictionlessly down an incline $\alpha$ ($a_0 = g\sin\alpha$): $\boxed{g_{\text{eff}} = g\cos\alpha}$.
  • 4. Bob of density $\rho$ submerged in non-viscous liquid of density $\sigma$: $\boxed{g_{\text{eff}} = g\left(1 - \frac{\sigma}{\rho}\right)}$.
  • 5. Pendulum of Very Large Length ($L$ comparable to Earth's Radius $R = 6400\text{ km}$):
    $$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{g\left(\frac{1}{L} + \frac{1}{R}\right)}}} \qquad \left(\text{For } L \to \infty: \; T_{\max} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g}} \approx 84.6\text{ minutes!}\right)$$
4.2 Compound (Physical) Pendulum & Classic Mechanical SHM Systems
Compound / Physical Pendulum:
Any rigid body of mass $m$ suspended from a horizontal pivot at distance $d$ from its Center of Mass ($I = I_{\text{cm}} + md^2 = m(k^2 + d^2)$):
$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I_{\text{pivot}}}{m g d}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\frac{k^2}{d} + d}{g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L_{\text{eq}}}{g}}} \qquad \left(\text{Equivalent Length } L_{\text{eq}} = d + \frac{k^2}{d}\right)$$
Physical SystemRestoring Force / TorqueTime Period Formula ($T$)
1. Liquid Column of Total Length $L$ in a Vertical U-TubeWeight of unbalanced height $2y$: $F = -(2A\rho g)y$$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{2g}}}$$
2. Tunnel Dug Through the Earth (Along Diameter OR Any Chord!)Inside Earth, $F_r = -\frac{GMm}{R^3}r$, so $F_x = -\left(\frac{mg}{R}\right)x$$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g}} \approx 84.6\text{ min}}$$
3. Floating Cylinder / Block (Submerged depth $h$ at equilibrium)Extra buoyant force $F = -A\rho_L g y$ while $m = A h \rho_L$$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{h}{g}}}$$
4. Torsional Pendulum (Twisting wire with torsional constant $C$)Restoring torque $\tau = -C\theta = I\alpha$$$\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{C}}}$$
4.3 Damped Oscillations & Forced Resonance

When a resistive damping force $F_d = -bv$ acts alongside $-kx$, the equation of motion is $m\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + b\frac{dv}{dt} + kx = 0$. For weak damping, amplitude decays exponentially:

$$\boxed{x(t) = A_0 e^{-\frac{bt}{2m}}\cos(\omega' t + \phi)} \implies \textbf{Amplitude:} \; A(t) = A_0 e^{-\frac{bt}{2m}}, \quad \textbf{Energy:} \; E(t) = E_0 e^{-\frac{bt}{m}}$$

where $\omega' = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m} - \left(\frac{b}{2m}\right)^2}$. Under a periodic driving force $F(t) = F_0\cos(\omega_d t)$, amplitude peaks sharply when driving frequency matches natural frequency ($\omega_d \approx \omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$), a phenomenon called Resonance.
topics.derivationHtml:
Proof of SHM inside Any Straight Tunnel (Chord) Dug Through the Earth

Suppose a straight frictionless tunnel is dug along a chord of the Earth at perpendicular distance $d$ from Earth's center. When a particle of mass $m$ is at distance $x$ from the midpoint of the tunnel (so its radial distance from Earth's center is $r = \sqrt{x^2 + d^2}$), the gravitational pull toward Earth's center is $F_{\text{grav}} = \frac{GMm}{R^3}r = \frac{mg}{R}r$.

The component of this force parallel to the tunnel pointing back toward the midpoint is:

$$F_x = -F_{\text{grav}}\cos\theta = -\left(\frac{mg}{R}r\right)\left(\frac{x}{r}\right) = -\left(\frac{mg}{R}\right)x \implies a_x = -\left(\frac{g}{R}\right)x$$

Notice that both $r$ and $d$ cancel out completely! Therefore, $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{g}{R}}$ and $\boxed{T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R}{g}} \approx 84.6\text{ min}}$ for EVERY straight tunnel through the Earth!

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Damped SHM Amplitude vs. Energy Half-Life): Since $A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/(2m)}$ while $E(t) \propto A^2 = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$, Mechanical Energy decays TWICE as fast in the exponent as Amplitude! If amplitude becomes $\frac{1}{2}A_0$ in $10\text{ s}$, energy becomes $\frac{1}{4}E_0$ in $10\text{ s}$ (and $\frac{1}{2}E_0$ in just $5\text{ s}$)!
  • Trap 2 (Simple Pendulum Length $L$ Is Measured to the Center of Mass of the Bob!): If a hollow spherical bob filled with water slowly leaks water from a tiny hole at the bottom, the Center of Mass of the bob first shifts downward ($L$ increases $\implies T$ increases), and once all water drains out, the COM returns to the center of the sphere ($L$ decreases back to original $\implies T$ returns to original value)!

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 13: Oscillations (Simple Harmonic Motion)! Every oscillatory tool—from phasor circles and reduced mass to physical pendulums and damped resonance—is now ready for Wave Mechanics in Chapter 14.
summary:
• SHM Kinematics: $a = -\omega^2 x$, $v = \pm\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}$, $x(t) = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$.
  • Energy in SHM: $E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$; $K = U$ at $x = \pm A/\sqrt{2}$; $K$ and $U$ oscillate at frequency $2f$.
  • Spring Systems: Parallel $k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$; Series $\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$; Cutting $kL = \text{const}$; Two-body $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
  • Pendulums: Simple $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g_{\text{eff}}}$; Compound $T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(mgd)}$.
  • Damped SHM: $A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/(2m)}$ and $E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$.
formulaSheetHtml:
System / ConceptMaster FormulaKey Shortcut
Velocity & Accel. in SHM$v = \pm\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}, \quad a = -\omega^2 x$$v_{\max} = A\omega$ at mean; $a_{\max} = A\omega^2$ at extreme.
Phasor Time Intervals$0 \to A/2: \; \dfrac{T}{12}, \qquad A/2 \to A: \; \dfrac{T}{6}$$0 \to A/\sqrt{2}$ takes $\dfrac{T}{8}$ (where $K = U$).
Spring Cutting ($m : n$)$k_1 = \left(\dfrac{m+n}{m}\right)k, \quad k_2 = \left(\dfrac{m+n}{n}\right)k$Derived from $k L = \text{Constant}$.
Physical Pendulum$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I_{\text{pivot}}}{mgd}}$For uniform rod of length $L$ pivoted at end: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{2L}{3g}}$.
Damped Amplitude & Energy$A(t) = A_0 e^{-bt/(2m)}, \quad E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$If $A \to A_0/e$ in $\tau$, then $E \to E_0/e^2$ in $\tau$.

questions.prompt: A particle executes Simple Harmonic Motion with an amplitude $A = 10\text{ cm}$ and time period $T = 6\text{ s}$. What is the minimum time required for the particle to move from its mean position ($x = 0$) to a point $x = 5\text{ cm}$ ($A/2$)?
questions.explanation: From $x = 0$ to $x = A/2$, the phase angle traveled on the reference circle is $\Delta\theta = \arcsin(1/2) = \frac{\pi}{6}$. Thus $t = \frac{T}{12} = \frac{6\text{ s}}{12} = 0.5\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: At what displacement $x$ from the mean position is the kinetic energy of a simple harmonic oscillator exactly equal to three times its potential energy ($K = 3U$, assuming $U(0) = 0$)?
questions.explanation: Since $K + U = E = \frac{1}{2}kA^2$ and $K = 3U$, we have $4U = E \implies 4\left(\frac{1}{2}kx^2\right) = \frac{1}{2}kA^2 \implies x^2 = \frac{A^2}{4} \implies x = \pm\frac{A}{2}$.

questions.prompt: A uniform spring of force constant $k$ is cut into two pieces whose lengths are in the ratio $1 : 2$. If the longer piece is now attached to a block of mass $m$, what is the new force constant $k_2$ of this longer piece?
questions.explanation: The longer piece has length $L_2 = \frac{2}{1+2}L = \frac{2}{3}L$. Since $k L = k_2 L_2 = \text{constant}$, we get $k_2 = k\left(\frac{L}{L_2}\right) = \frac{3}{2}k$.

questions.prompt: A simple pendulum has a time period $T_1$ when on the Earth's surface, and $T_2$ when taken to a height $h = R$ above the Earth's surface (where $R$ is the radius of the Earth). The value of the ratio $\frac{T_2}{T_1}$ is:
questions.explanation: At height $h = R$, distance from Earth's center is $r = 2R$, so $g' = \frac{g}{(1 + R/R)^2} = \frac{g}{4}$. Since $T \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}$, we get $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{g'}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$.

questions.prompt: A thin uniform rod of length $L = 1.5\text{ m}$ is pivoted at one of its ends so that it can oscillate freely in a vertical plane as a physical pendulum. What is its time period of small oscillations? ($g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$)
questions.explanation: For a rod pivoted at one end, $I_{\text{pivot}} = \frac{1}{3}mL^2$ and distance of COM from pivot is $d = \frac{L}{2}$. Thus $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\frac{1}{3}mL^2}{mg(L/2)}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2L}{3g}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{2(1.5)}{3(10)}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{3}{30}} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.1}\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: In a damped oscillator, the mass of the block is $m = 200\text{ g}$, spring constant $k = 90\text{ N/m}$, and damping constant $b = 40\text{ g/s}$. How much time does it take for its mechanical energy to drop to $\frac{1}{e}$ of its initial value?
questions.explanation: Mechanical energy decays as $E(t) = E_0 e^{-bt/m}$. For $E(t) = \frac{E_0}{e} = E_0 e^{-1}$, we set $\frac{bt}{m} = 1 \implies t = \frac{m}{b} = \frac{200\text{ g}}{40\text{ g/s}} = 5\text{ s}$.

questions.prompt: Two blocks of masses $m_1 = 3\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 6\text{ kg}$ rest on a smooth horizontal table and are connected by a light spring of stiffness $k = 200\text{ N/m}$. If the blocks are pulled apart slightly and released, what is the angular frequency $\omega$ of their oscillation?
questions.explanation: Reduced mass of the two-block system is $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{3 \times 6}{3 + 6} = \frac{18}{9} = 2\text{ kg}$. Therefore, $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{200}{2}} = \sqrt{100} = 10\text{ rad/s}$.
